title: Brookhaven: Expanding Claims and Retained Native Land
summary: Brookhaven’s colonial claim expanded through purchases and patents across Setalcott and Unkechaug homelands. The records also promise planting land and resource rights to Native families and their heirs.

why_this_matters: Land loss was a process involving agreements, contested claims, colonial institutions and restrictions on Native access. Read the actors, obligations and continuing communities together; a broad outline does not mean every Native right ended on one date.
introduction_title: Native homeland, colonial claims and continuing rights
introduction_content: Brookhaven’s colonial claim expanded through purchases and patents across Setalcott and Unkechaug homelands. The records also promise planting land and resource rights to Native families and their heirs.
history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
Two shores, several transactions

Brookhaven spans the north and south shores of central Long Island. Its colonial boundaries brought together lands associated with Setalcott and Unkechaug people; they were not one empty tract transferred on a single date. The initial English settlement at Setauket in 1655 was much smaller than the later town. Further agreements and colonial patents expanded the claim. Growth of Brookhaven

A patent anticipated land not yet purchased

Governor Richard Nicolls's 1666 patent is especially revealing. It confirmed land already purchased and also land that might be purchased later from Native proprietors or others. It described a broad north-to-south jurisdiction. The patent therefore describes a colonial claim and framework for future acquisition; it does not establish that every Native owner had already sold, or that all Native rights ended in 1666. Records of the Town of Brookhaven, up to 1800

Gie, Woodhull and the North Purchase

The November 19, 1675 North Purchase documents show how that expansion worked. Gie, a Setauket sachem, and his associates confirmed earlier purchases between Stony Brook and Wading River, from the Sound to the middle of the island. The deed also conveyed the interests described as not yet purchased to Richard Woodhull. On November 23, Woodhull assigned his interest to Brookhaven's inhabitants. The town awarded him a farm and meadow interest at Wading River in consideration of that assignment. The record thus identifies an intermediary and his benefit, not merely an anonymous change of ownership. Records of the Town of Brookhaven, up to 1800

The promise to Native families

An accompanying promise is indispensable to understanding the transaction. Brookhaven's inhabitants undertook to provide sufficient planting land for Gie and his associates, described as the true Native proprietors, and for their heirs. They also promised freedom to hunt, fish and fowl within Setauket's bounds. The same record that supports the colonial claim preserves obligations to continuing Native families. It cannot honestly be presented as proof that those families had left or abandoned the place. Records of the Town of Brookhaven, up to 1800

Restricted planting lands on the south shore

The south shore had its own agreements and constraints. A July 2, 1700 instrument by William Smith recited earlier purchases from Tobaguss and other Unkechaug possessors and set aside planting land at several named places. Its total of 175 acres was distributed among several tracts, not a surveyed description of today's Poospatuck reservation. It restricted alienation and reserved the use of the ground after crops were removed to Smith, while requiring an annual corn payment. This illustrates how retained land could exist within a larger colonial estate under restrictive conditions. Records of the Town of Brookhaven, up to 1800

Communities that continued

The continuing Unkechaug community at Poospatuck and the Setalcott homeland must remain part of the map's account. Land loss changed control and access; it did not make people or their relationships to land vanish. Follow the linked community articles for present-day histories. The colonial documents here establish specific claims and promises, not a complete account of every family's experience or the later enforcement of every right. Records of the Town of Brookhaven, up to 1800

Continue with Unkechaug Indian Reservation, Unkechaug Ancestral Land and Setalcott history.
whereintheworld_content:
This is a regional reading area based on the present-day Town of Brookhaven, with modern shoreline and water clipping. It is not the footprint of the smaller 1655 purchase, the 1675 North Purchase, or a single completed land transfer. The 1666 patent included land that might be purchased later. Kavenagh’s map 11 distinguishes several acquisitions within the region. Present-day Poospatuck Indian Territory is excluded from the shaded area using NYS mapping to keep retained Native land visible. That opening shows retained land today, not the several tracts described by the 1700 instrument or their historic acreage.
